newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia miners see "sun shining on uranium".
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia miners see "sun shining on uranium".

text.p: DARWIN, Feb 24 ( Reuter) - Planned development of new Australian uranium mines and the upgrading of existing major mines is proceeding strongly after the demise of Australia's "three-mines" policy, a uranium conference here heard on Monday.
"The sun is shining on uranium," Ian Hoare-Lacey, general manager of the Uranium Information Centre Ltd, said in opening remarks at the conference.

Energy Resources of Australia Ltd hopes to have full approval by the end of this year to bring its long-mooted Jabiluka mine in Australia's Northern Teritory into production by 1999 or 2000 at about 1,000 tonnes a year of uranium oxide, chief executive, Phil Shirvington told Reuters.
With production from its Ranger mine, this would give ERA total annual production of 6,000 tonnes of uranium oxide (U308).

Australia's other major existing producer, WMC Ltd is confident it will secure new uranium contracts to absorb expanded output, James Eggins, general manager, marketing for copper and uranium for WMC, said.
WMC is spending A$1.49 billion to boost annual production at its Olympic Dam uranium project in South Australia to 3,700 tonnes by the end of the decade from 1,500 tonnes now.

French-owned Cogema Australia Pty Ltd, which owns the Koongarra uranium deposit 35 kms south of Ranger, is reassessing the feasibility of the long-dormant project, Francois Bautin, managing director of Coongarra Mines said.
RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd's Kintyre uranium prospect in Western Australia could be in production by the second half of 1999, Bruce Larson, a spokesman for RTZ-CRA said.
"A resource of 36,000 tonnes of U3O8 has been estimated in the immediate Kintyre area while drilling had identified an indicated resource of 24,000 tonnes," he said.
Development requires all regulatory approvals to be in place by 1997, he said.
Two more uranium deposits in the Lake Frome area of South Australia has the potential for mining, David Brunt, of DSJ Consulting Services said.
The larger prospect, Beverly, contains about 11,600 tonnes of U3O8 and is being "actively progressed" to a mine capable of yielding 900 tonnes a year by 2000, he said.
The prospect is owned by General Atomics Corp of the U.S.
The second prospect, Honeymoon, contains reserves 3,360 tonnes and is owned by Canada's Southern Cross Resources Inc, part-owned by Australian-listed Sedimentary Holdings NL.
Southern Cross planned to revive the project to establish commercial production in 1999, Brunt said.
At predicted world uranium prices of around US$15-$18 a pound, all Australia's new mines "looked to be very profitable," ERA's Shirvington said.

The new conservative Australian government scrapped the former Labor government's three mines policy after it won power in 1996, opening the door for development of long-discovered deposits that had been languishing on the shelf and for expansion of existing ones.
